title: Dew Drop owners and the eight and twelve dollar pay scale
summary: The Panniers ran the Dew Drop; musicians were paid either eight or twelve dollars a night depending on reading ability.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Here comes Pat. And, uh, that was at the Dewdrop. Now, the Dewdrop, I don't know how many stories you've heard about the Dewdrop and how it, uh, was in operation. But it was run by, uh, three brothers, mainly by Frank Pannier, uh, Joe Pannier and his brother, uh, Paul. Paul. Paul. Paul. Paul fed us. Frank worked us. Oh, yeah. Because Frank ran the, uh, entertainment part of it, you see. He booked bands, and he ran the hotel, and he ran the club, you know. And, uh, in those days, uh, there were two, uh, two types of musicians. Those who got paid $8 a night, and those who got paid $12 a night.
What was, what was the difference?

I don't really, well, he, I think he did it in the quality of the musician. If the musician was a, of the high quality reading popular thing. Let me, let me show you the difference. Okay. And I'm not ashamed to say that I played that for $8, and I graduated to $12, you know. But it's people like, uh, Red Tyler. Sure. Uh, and all those people who, uh, much older and veterans of, uh, World War II, and came from gateways and Groomwall School of Music and so forth. Ernest McElaine, the Davises. They're, uh, rocking on name and names. They got the $12. They worked the same time as us, you know, from sundown to sunup. You know what I'm saying? And they got the same drinks as us. Yeah. That good syrup, wine, you know. Yeah. But they made like $4 a night more than us. Uh-huh. And then a gig that, in those days, you made, uh, well, $36 a week playing the music. It was good.
